nameStory: The 'sensitive pea' gets its name from its remarkable ability to quickly fold its leaflets together when touched, making it seem shy or sensitive to contact. This dramatic response to touch is called 'thigmonasty' and helps protect the delicate leaves from damage by animals or harsh weather.
description: Sensitive pea is a small annual wildflower in the legume family that grows low to the ground in spreading patches. It produces delicate, feathery compound leaves made up of many tiny leaflets that dramatically fold closed when disturbed. The plant reaches only 6-20 inches tall and bears small yellow flowers followed by slender seed pods typical of the pea family.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery compound leaves with 10-20 pairs of tiny, oblong leaflets that instantly fold together when touched - like a plant version of 'playing dead'

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow flowers about 1/4 inch across with 5 petals, appearing singly or in small clusters along the stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that spreads in branching mats close to the ground, rarely exceeding knee height

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Thin, flat seed pods about 1-2 inches long that split open when ripe, releasing small brown seeds with a smooth, hard texture

habitat: Look for sensitive pea in sunny, disturbed areas with sandy or poor soils throughout New England - roadsides, old fields, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. It thrives in areas with full sun and well-drained soils where competition from other plants is reduced.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soils warm, with first feathery leaves appearing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid-summer through early fall, with the touch-sensitive leaves at their most responsive during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open in early fall, releasing next year's generation before the first frost kills the annual plants.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence - exists only as dormant seeds in the soil waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: Scientists believe the rapid leaf-folding response evolved as a defense mechanism - when the leaves suddenly collapse, it startles browsing animals and may make the plant look wilted or unappetizing, causing the animal to move on to seemingly 'healthier' plants nearby.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small legumes in disturbed areas, but the instant leaf-folding response when touched is a dead giveaway - no other common New England plant reacts so dramatically to gentle contact.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sensitive pea,' this plant isn't closely related to garden peas - it's in a different genus within the large legume family. The 'pea' name comes from its similar seed pods and ability to fix nitrogen in the soil like other legumes.
compareHints: Sensitive pea is much smaller and more delicate than its close relative partridge pea, which grows taller with larger flowers and leaflets that are less sensitive to touch. Partridge pea also tends to be more robust and upright, while sensitive pea stays low and spreading.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Partridge pea is much showier than its cousin sensitive pea, with flowers nearly ten times larger and more vibrant yellow petals.
